title: Symmetry and Quantum Geometry in Bloch Bands
authors: Ziwei Wang, Charlie Raca, Steven H. Simon
abstract: Quantum geometric quantities have featured heavily in the discussion of the properties of quantum systems in recent years. Among quantities most commonly discussed is the variance of Berry curvature and the integral of the trace of the quantum metric tensor. Despite their usefulness, it is known that they suffer from one significant complication: for a tight-binding model, the quantum geometric quantities depend not only on the parameters of the tight-binding model itself, but also the real space geometry of the tight-binding model, the so-called "orbital embedding". One explicitly geometry-independent quantity is therefore the minimal value of the quantum geometric quantity out of all possible real space geometries. In this work, we demonstrate that, if the tight-binding model is compatible with certain spatial symmetries, then the real space geometry that minimizes the variance of the Berry curvature or the integral of the trace of the quantum metric tensor must obey all those spatial symmetries. We further show that the statement is applicable to systems with magnetic translation symmetries and other composite symmetries, with implications for the quantum geometry of the Hofstadter model.
summary: This paper investigates quantum geometric quantities derived from Bloch bands, which typically depend on both model parameters and the specific real-space arrangement of orbitals. The authors show that if the system possesses underlying spatial symmetries, the geometry that minimizes key measures like Berry curvature variance must itself obey those symmetries. This provides a powerful symmetry constraint for understanding quantum geometry in crystalline solids.
main_problem: The authors aim to find an explicit, geometry-independent measure for quantum geometric quantities (like Berry curvature variance or integrated quantum metric) in tight-binding models.
main_result: They prove that if the underlying tight-binding model possesses certain spatial symmetries, then the real-space geometry that minimizes these quantum geometric measures must necessarily respect those same spatial symmetries.
method: The work uses minimization arguments over the space of possible real-space embeddings (orbital positions) for a given lattice structure to constrain the optimal geometry.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Bloch bands described by tight-binding models, initially in two dimensions and generalized to include magnetic translation symmetries. The analysis involves optimizing quantities related to the Berry curvature and quantum metric tensor.
key_observables: Berry curvature ($\Omega$), Quantum metric tensor ($g_{ij}$), Integrated quantum metric ($I$), and Variance of Berry curvature ($\sigma^2_\Omega$).
important_parameters: Spatial symmetries, magnetic flux parameters (related to the Hofstadter model), and lattice geometry/orbital embedding $\{r_{a,i}\}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that a global minimum for the geometric quantities exists in the space of embeddings, and it extends symmetry considerations to include gauge transformations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the honeycomb lattice structure used as an example system.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of geometry dependence. It then details the mathematical setup using quantum geometric tensors ($Q_{ij}, g_{ij}, \Omega$). The core argument demonstrates that symmetry dictates the minimal geometry, extending this principle to magnetic and composite symmetries, concluding with implications for models like the Hofstadter model.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between fundamental physical symmetries (like spatial or magnetic translation symmetries) and the minimization of geometric invariants is a powerful tool for constraining theoretical models in condensed matter physics.
